name: Dark Vinaceous-Drab
lede: Dark Vinaceous-Drab is a grayish yellowish brown from Ridgway's 1912 dictionary, combining his wine-colored *vinaceous* with a dull *drab*, and it shares its exact hex with another of our names, Mole brown.

sections.title: A compound, documented name
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 dictionary lists Dark Vinaceous-Drab at #76665E, plate XLV, hue 5″″, tone i, and the ISCC-NBS circular of 1955 files it as "grayish red" [1]. The name compounds two documented Latin-derived words: *vinaceous*, wine-colored, and *drab*, an old word for the dull, undyed brown of raw wool or linen [1]. Together they describe a muted, wine-tinged brown rather than naming any plant, place or person [1].

In our color graph the exact same hex is also cataloged under [[mole-brown|Mole brown]], two names for one identical swatch [1]. The nearest distinct neighbor is [[plain-mouse|Plain mouse]], 3.0 units away [1]. The swatch sits with our [[brown|brown]] family, its gray and yellow modifiers also pulling it toward [[grey|grey]] and [[yellow|yellow]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 3.49% of 23,781 paintings, 830 of them, as photographed, with the within-painting lens counting 444[2]. That is more common than 81% of our named colors [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 5.0% of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 2.1 times the rate its museums would predict [2]. Within a painting it most often sits as a mid-tone, in 28% of its 444 appearances [2]. Theodor Philipsen is its most devoted painter, holding it in 6 of 28 works here, 3.7 times the baseline of the museums his paintings come from [2]. It is most over-represented in Nepal, 6.1 times the expected rate [2]. It shares canvases with [[pale-taupe|Pale taupe]] and [[taupe-brown|Taupe Brown]] far more often than chance, at 13.3 and 9.3 times the expected rate [2]. The earliest match dates to 1000, 912 years before Ridgway recorded the name, a floor rather than a first [2].
